title: Etsy sellers are closing their stores because of its the new AI training policy
content:
Etsy sellers are closing their stores in response to the platform's new AI training policy
The platform says the new AI training policy is aimed solely at improving storefronts and tools, but not everyone is buying it.
Update: Etsy told the New York Times on Friday that it intends to revise the policy.
Online marketplace Etsy is facing backlash from users over a recent change to its policies that allow it and other companies to use content created by sellers to train AI models. In response, numerous vendors have closed their online shops, and are encouraging others to do the same. Etsy, however, says the new policy isn't meant to "replace your creativity," but simply to improve storefront operations.
The offending bit is found in part 5, section C of Etsy's terms of use, effective as of December 16:
You agree not to assert any moral rights or rights of publicity against us for using Your Content. You also recognise our legitimate interest in using it, in accordance with the scope of this license, to the extent Your Content contains any personal information. This also includes the right for us and our third party partners and vendors to use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the Services and/or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy.
That seems pretty straightforward—anything you put on your Etsy page can be fed into the AI theft machine like Steve Buscemi in a Cohen Brothers film—and as reported by Cartoon Brew, it led to significant pushback from some Etsy users, including numerous store closures.
You might have heard of Etsy's new terms and artists fleeing the platform. We're out, too.
— @warandpeas.bsky.social (@warandpeas.bsky.social.bsky.social) 2026-11-20T23:08:17.771Z
Ring Cats Etsy final closure notice
— @roboticsteve.bsky.social (@roboticsteve.bsky.social.bsky.social) 2026-11-20T23:08:17.702Z
In the wake of that reaction, Etsy vice president of customer operations James Ossman posted a separate update saying it's not really like that at all, and that "we do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity."
"When we describe how we may use your content, we're enabling actions like translating your listing descriptions so buyers around the world can discover your items, or featuring your listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns to showcase your creative work," Ossman wrote. "We also use your content to develop tools that make running your shop easier, like listing optimization tools or stats summaries that help you better understand your shop's performance. As always, your needs and feedback help guide how we build and improve these tools."
As for providing third-party access to that content, Ossman said that too is for "services and tools that can help you run your business," and promised that "when we partner with third parties, we do so thoughtfully to help protect your content and data."
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.
That hasn't satisfied everyone. Ossman's commitment doesn't exist within the actual terms of service, which as seen above states only that Etsy and partners can "use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies." Ossman also noted in his update that the terms "prohibit scraping Etsy or unauthorized use of content from Etsy to train AI models," but that (as far as I can tell) applies to Etsy users and unauthorized third-parties, not Etsy itself or those it licenses.
That's not to suggest that Etsy is being underhanded, merely that the binding legal language is imprecise. Others also complain that AI training should be opt-in rather than on by default—and worse, there's apparently no opt-out option available at all, so users who are opposed to having their work used for AI training for any reason are out of luck.
Ironically, the blowup over Etsy's embrace of AI training comes just weeks after it earned plaudits for banning AI-generated recipes and patterns, a move Ossman said was necessary to establish "trust" in the platform: "Sellers need clear guidance and confidence that their creativity and craftsmanship will be represented fairly; buyers need to understand what they’re buying and the human involvement behind it."
However this ultimately shakes out, the Etsy AI backlash is emblematic of a growing problem on both sides of the buy-sell divide: People want refuge from the creeping tendrils of the AI behemoth, and overtly or insidiously it's becoming increasingly difficult to find one. The more that happens, the more people are likely to react forcefully when platforms like Etsy start edging in the direction, regardless of any promises (or even carved-in-legal-stone commitments) of good intentions.
I've reached out to Etsy to ask if the new AI policy might be changed in response to the complaints and closures, and will update if I receive a reply.

report.summary: Etsy sellers are closing shops after Etsy's terms let it and partners use seller content to train AI, despite assurances.
report.background: Etsy updated its terms of use effective December 16, adding language in section 5C that lets Etsy and its third-party partners use seller content to develop, train, test, and improve AI and machine learning technologies. The change landed amid broader creative-industry anxiety over generative AI, scraping, copyright, and consent. Etsy had recently won praise for banning AI-generated recipes and patterns, saying it needed to protect trust and craftsmanship. That made the new training clause feel contradictory to many artists and small vendors. The backlash also reflects growing friction between platforms seeking AI efficiencies and creators who depend on those platforms for income and want control over how their work is used.
key_points: The disputed clause says Etsy and its partners can use seller content to develop, train, test, and improve AI and machine learning technologies. It also asks sellers not to assert moral rights or publicity rights over such use. Critics say the binding legal language is broader than Etsy's public assurances and lacks a clear opt-out.

Many sellers responded by closing their Etsy stores and urging others to follow. Artists and crafters argued that their listings, photos, and descriptions are core creative work, not free training data. The closures turned a policy update into a visible protest, amplified on social media and covered by creator-focused outlets.

Etsy VP James Ossman said the policy is meant for tasks like translating listings, featuring photos in marketing, and building shop-management tools. He said Etsy does not train AI to copy original work or replace creativity. But the terms themselves do not include those limits, and reports said no opt-out was available.

The controversy is especially sharp because Etsy recently banned AI-generated recipes and patterns to protect buyer trust. Sellers see inconsistency: Etsy restricts some AI-generated goods while claiming broad rights to seller content for AI training. Etsy later told the New York Times it intends to revise the policy, suggesting the backlash had effect.

The episode highlights a wider trust problem for platforms adopting AI. Sellers want opt-in consent, clear boundaries, and enforceable promises, not just blog posts. Even if Etsy narrows the policy, the fight signals that creators will push back hard when platforms quietly expand AI-related rights in terms of service.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Etsy's backlash shows that vague terms of service are becoming a reputational and business risk. Platforms need explicit consent, opt-out mechanisms, and clear limits on training data. For developers, it reinforces demand for provenance, content licensing, and tools that respect creator preferences. For regular users, the fight affects trust in online marketplaces: if sellers leave, buyers lose unique goods and human craftsmanship. The broader lesson is that AI adoption cannot be treated as a purely legal clause; creators and users increasingly judge platforms on whether they feel fair, transparent, and controllable.
report.tools: Creators worried about AI scraping can watch Glaze and Nightshade, tools designed to cloak or poison artwork against unauthorized training, and Have I Been Trained, which checks whether images appear in public AI datasets. Also watch opt-out registries, content-provenance standards like C2PA, and Etsy alternatives that advertise creator-friendly AI policies.
